title: Paiwan in Progress
bodyHtml:
Paiwan is the language of the Paiwan people, one of the indigenous peoples of Taiwan. There are nearly 100,000 Paiwan people, and approximately 15,000 of them are native speakers of the language.

Below are some Paiwan verbs given in two forms: their root form and their progressive form. (The root form is a verb's basic form, and the progressive is the form that, in English, has the ending -ing.) The meanings of the verbs are provided for interest, but they are not necessary for solving the problem.

F1. Some entries in the table have been left blank. Fill them in on your Answer Sheet.

Root FormsProgressive Forms
kemanto eatkemakaneating
ivuto talkivuivutalking
kivatato askkivatavataasking
lemumayto hitlemumalumayhitting
temekelto drinktemeketekeldrinking
kalidjikidjto flashkalidjikidjikidjflashing
paderuato hiccuppaderuaruahiccupping
semutjirayto spitsemutjiratjirayspitting
kemesato cookkemesakesacooking
temuluto teachteaching
djemavacto walkwalking
lemenguaqto fixfixing
mikerekelto shakeshaking
takalavato waitwaiting
masasevalitto take a turntaking turns

questions.partPrompt: Some entries in the table have been left blank. Fill in the missing progressive forms.

questions.promptHtml: (f) Progressive form of masasevalit (to take a turn)

hints.text: Every progressive form is longer than its root because a chunk of the root is repeated (this is called reduplication). Line the two forms up letter by letter from the END of the word and mark exactly which letters got copied.

The copied chunk always stretches back to the second-to-last vowel of the word, and any word-final consonant stays at the very end. But watch the words containing me or em right after the first consonant, like kemesa or temekel: that little syllable behaves like an extra piece that the copy skips over.

Work through semutjiray, which is already given. Ignore the -em- to get sutjiray. Counting vowels from the right, the last two are i and a, so the chunk from the second-to-last vowel's consonant onward is tjira. Insert that copy right after the last vowel, keeping the final y at the end: semutjira + tjira + y gives semutjiratjiray, exactly the form in the table.

explanationHtml:
Step 1: Find what is being repeated

Compare each root with its progressive. In every pair the progressive is the root with an extra chunk stuffed into it, and the chunk is a copy of material already in the word. Linguists call this reduplication: repeating part of a word to signal a grammatical meaning (here, the ongoing "-ing" sense).

RootProgressive, split upCopied chunk
kivatakivata + vatavata
paderuapaderua + ruarua
kalidjikidjkalidjiki + djiki + djdjiki
temekeltemeke + teke + lteke

Step 2: Where does the copy start and where does it go?

Count vowels from the right. In kivata the last two vowels are the a of va and the final a; the copy vata begins with the consonant that sits in front of the second-to-last vowel. Same in kalidjikidj: last two vowels are i and i, and the copy starts at dji.

The copy is placed right after the last vowel of the word. If the word ends in a consonant, that consonant simply stays at the very end, so it looks as though the copy was slipped in just before it: kalidjiki-djiki-dj, temeke-teke-l. If the word ends in a vowel, the copy just goes on the end: kivata-vata.

Step 3: The tricky words with -em-

Some forms look like they break the rule. kemesa should give kemesamesa, but the real answer is kemesakesa. Likewise keman gives kemakan, not kemakeman, and lemumay gives lemumalumay.

The explanation: these verbs contain an infix - a piece of grammar inserted inside the word rather than at the front or back. Here it is -em-, slotted in after the first consonant. Strip it out and you recover the bare stem:

keman
k-em-an, stem kan
kemesa
k-em-esa, stem kesa
lemumay
l-em-umay, stem lumay
temekel
t-em-ekel, stem tekel
semutjiray
s-em-utjiray, stem sutjiray

The copy is taken from the stem, ignoring the -em-, and then dropped into the full word after its last vowel. So kemesa copies kesa from the stem: kemesa + kesa. And keman copies ka (the stem kan minus its final consonant): kema + ka + n.

Step 4: Apply it to the blanks

  • temulu: contains -em-, stem tulu. Copy tulu after the last vowel: temulutulu.
  • djemavac: stem djavac. Copy djava, final c stays last: djemavadjavac.
  • lemenguaq: stem lenguaq. The last two vowels are u and a, so the copy is ngua, with final q at the end: lemenguanguaq.
  • mikerekel: no -em- infix here (the mi- is a prefix, not an infix). Last two vowels e, e, so the copy is reke: mikerekerekel.
  • takalava: no infix, copy lava, word ends in a vowel: takalavalava.
  • masasevalit: no infix, copy vali, final t stays last: masasevalivalit.

One more check on how to count syllables: in paderua the sequence ua is two vowels, so the last two vowels are u and a and the copy is rua - the same reasoning that gives ngua in lemenguaq.
